questions.q:
Convert the denary number 183 into:
(a) 8-bit binary [1]
(b) hexadecimal. [1]
questions.tip: Check your binary by adding the place values back up before converting to hex.

questions.q:
The hexadecimal number 3E9 is stored in a computer.
(a) Convert 3E9 to denary. [1]
(b) Convert 3E9 to 12-bit binary. [1]
questions.tip: Each hex digit is exactly 4 bits – keep the leading zeros.

questions.q:
Add the 8-bit binary numbers 10011101 and 01101011. Show your working.
Give the 8-bit result and explain what has happened.
ms: the result (264) is greater than 255 / needs 9 bits, so the 9th bit / carry is lost (1)
questions.model:
10011101
+ 01101011
  --------
 100001000 (carries in every column from bit 0 to bit 7)
The 8-bit result is 00001000. An overflow error has occurred: 157 + 107 = 264, which is larger than 255, the largest number that can be stored in 8 bits. The 9th bit (the final carry) cannot be stored and is lost, so the stored result (8) is wrong.
questions.tip: Always check the answer in denary: 157 + 107 = 264 > 255 means overflow.

questions.q:
The 8-bit register holds 00110100.
(a) Perform a logical right shift of 2 places. Give the result in binary and its denary value. [2]
(b) The original value 00110100 is instead shifted left 3 places. Give the result and explain why it is not 8 times the original value. [2]
ms: (b) 1s are shifted out of the most significant end / bits are lost, so the result is 160 not 416 (8 × 52)
questions.model:
(a) 00110100 shifted right 2 → 00001101, which is 13. The original was 52, so it has been divided by 4.
(b) 00110100 shifted left 3 → 10100000 (160). 8 × 52 = 416, which needs more than 8 bits; the two 1s at the left were shifted out of the register and lost, so the answer is wrong.
questions.tip: In a logical shift, 0s fill the empty positions at the other end.

questions.q:
Two's complement is used to store integers in 8 bits.
(a) Show how −77 is stored in 8-bit two's complement. Show your working. [3]
(b) State the denary value of the two's complement number 11001010. [1]
(c) State the range of denary values that can be stored in 8-bit two's complement. [1]
ms: (a) M1: invert all bits (10110010) and add 1 / or −128 + 51
questions.tip: Check your answer by adding the place values with −128 for the leftmost bit.

questions.q:
An 8-bit register contains the bit pattern 11100110.
(a) State the denary value if it is an unsigned binary integer. [1]
(b) State the denary value if it is a two's complement integer. Show your working. [2]
(c) State the hexadecimal equivalent. [1]
(d) Give the result of a logical right shift of 1 place on the original pattern, and its unsigned denary value. [1]
(e) Explain why the same bit pattern can represent different values. [1]
ms: (e) the value depends on how the program / computer interprets the bits (unsigned, two's complement, character, colour …)
questions.model:
(a) 128 + 64 + 32 + 4 + 2 = 230.
(b) −128 + 64 + 32 + 4 + 2 = −26.
(c) 1110 = E, 0110 = 6, so E6.
(d) 01110011, which is 115 (230 ÷ 2).
(e) The bits themselves have no meaning; it is the way the program interprets them (unsigned, two's complement, ASCII, etc.) that decides the value.
